keys.{a_branching_school_story_you_play_toget: A branching school story you play together.
keys.{intro_line1}: One school year, told from one point of view - but every choice is decided by a
keys.{intro_line2}: vote of everyone in the lobby. Eight chapters, five people worth knowing, and
keys.{intro_line3}: nineteen different endings are on the table.
keys.{intro_line4}: When everyone has arrived, the host starts the story.
keys.{sd_a_back_n}: She hesitates for a long time, then turns to the back of the book and gives you exactly one page. It is Zeynep - mid-sentence, hands up, delighted. Drawn with enormous kindness. "I draw people when they forget to be watched," she says. "That is the only time anyone looks like themselves."
keys.{sd_a_cover_n}: You stay until the librarian starts turning off lamps as a hint. The work is good. Her half is better. At the bottom of her last page, in pencil so light you nearly miss it, she has written: thank you for not asking why I have to go.
keys.{sd_a_finish}: Three weeks later the project goes in. Her illustrations carry it and both your names are on the front, hers second, in letters half the size of yours. You ask her why. "Habit," she says, and does not change it.
keys.{sd_a_home_n}: Twelve minutes of walking and she talks for eleven of them, which you suspect is a personal record. Her mother is not cruel, she explains, carefully, twice. Her mother is frightened. "She grew up with nothing and I am asking to spend four years on paper." At her street she stops. "Do not come further."
keys.{sd_a_lib1_c0}: "They are not doodles. They are the best thing in this school."
keys.{sd_a_lib1_c2}: "Let us just split the workload evenly."
keys.{sd_a_lib1}: After class, the library. Aylin spreads out her sketches - they are extraordinary, and she clearly has no idea. "They are just doodles," she mumbles when she catches you staring.
keys.{sd_a_lib2_c0}: "I will walk you. We can talk on the way."
keys.{sd_a_lib2_c1}: "Go. I will finish tonight and you owe me nothing."
keys.{sd_a_lib2_c2}: "Tell her the truth. She is going to find out."
keys.{sd_a_lib2}: At half past five her phone buzzes and the whole shape of her changes. "I have to go. I am not - " she starts packing without folding anything " - I am supposed to be home by six. My mother thinks I stay late for maths." The sketchbook goes into her bag last, upside down, hidden under a textbook.
keys.{sd_a_praise_n}: For the first time, she looks right at you. Something in her face softens, then panics, then hides in the sketchbook. "...Thanks," she whispers. Then, so quietly you nearly miss it: "Nobody has said that out loud before."
keys.{sd_a_push_n}: "You think I have not tried?" It is the loudest she has been all year and it is barely above speaking. "You get to say things out loud. In my house there is one right answer and it is not mine." She goes. At the door she stops, and does not turn round. "...You are not wrong. That is the worst part."
keys.{sd_after_aylin}: She is on the rooftop with her phone face down on the concrete beside her and has been since twenty past nine. "I have not opened it," she says. "Two hours." She picks it up, and puts it down again. "Do not go anywhere. I am going to do it. I am. Just - do not go anywhere."
keys.{sd_after_deniz}: She is putting the two pages into a file with a completely steady hand. "I have 9-C in seven minutes and they are doing coordinates," she says, "and I intend to teach it very well, because that is the whole job and today I remembered that." At the door she stops. "It was the right size this time. Thank you for that."
keys.{sd_after_emre}: His mother shakes your hand with both of hers and says something in a voice too quiet to catch, and then goes to wait by the bus stop to give you the two minutes. Emre looks at the building. "Four years," he says. "I have never once stood on this side of the gate and looked at it."
keys.{sd_after_kerem}: He is standing in an empty classroom holding a printed slip and he has been standing there for some time. "Sixty-one," he says. "You need fifty." He reads it again. "I did that. Nobody read it to me and nobody gave me anything and I did that." His hands are not entirely steady. "Sixty-one."
keys.{sd_after_zeynep}: She is sitting in the middle of the yard, alone, eating lunch, in full view, with her back straight. "They are all looking," she says as you sit down. "They are." "I know." She takes a bite of her sandwich. "Turns out I can do that. Who knew."
keys.{sd_aylin_book}: "Oh - " She flips the page shut, then catches herself, then flips it back open at the same spot, embarrassed by her own reflex. "You can see this one. Just - " her thumb clamps the last third of the book " - not the back ones. The back ones are not finished."
keys.{sd_aylin_enters}: The door slides open. A girl with paint-stained fingers slips in, sketchbook hugged to her chest. Aylin. You would know her anywhere - and she never quite looks at anyone.
keys.{sd_aylin_first_c0}: Lean over. See what she is drawing.
keys.{sd_aylin_first_c2}: Leave her alone. She clearly wants that.
keys.{sd_aylin_first}: She takes the seat in front of yours because it is the seat nobody fights for. The sketchbook goes down. Her hand is already moving before she has fully sat.
keys.{sd_aylin_greet}: "Morning," she says to her desk. Then, half a second late, like she had to run the sentence twice to be sure it was allowed: "...Good morning." Her pencil has not stopped once.
keys.{sd_aylin_look}: It is the window. Just the window - the frame, the yard, the one branch that gets in the way of everything. Except she has drawn the branch as though it were the point and the school were the accident.
keys.{sd_ch1_end}: At the gate you look back. The building is dark except for one window on the ground floor - the office corridor, where the photocopier lives. Somebody is in there after hours, and the light goes out the moment you notice it.
keys.{sd_ch2_close}: The rooftop door has a sign on it that says NO ENTRY and a lock that has been broken since before any of you started here. Everyone knows. Nobody has ever reported it. It is the one place in the building where the school cannot see you, which is why, sooner or later, everybody ends up there.
keys.{sd_ch2_end}: Grades go up on the wall on Friday. Somewhere below the fold, three names have an asterisk beside them - resit required - and one of them belongs to somebody who has been laughing all week.
keys.{sd_ch2_open}: Second morning. Ms. Deniz walks the rows dealing out the project brief like cards. "Three weeks. Two names on the front. One grade for both of you." She pauses at your desk. "And before anyone asks - no, I will not tell you who to work with. That is the assessment."
keys.{sd_ch2_roof_c0}: Aylin. You told her where the door was.
keys.{sd_ch2_roof_c1}: Kerem. He brought food nobody asked for.
keys.{sd_ch2_roof_c2}: Emre. He was already here when you came up.
keys.{sd_ch2_roof_c3}: Zeynep. You invited her, which nobody does.
keys.{sd_ch2_roof_c4}: Nobody. That is the point of a roof.
keys.{sd_ch2_roof}: October. The city goes orange and the wind up here is already cold. Three weeks of work are over and you have earned one hour of doing nothing. Who is up here with you?
keys.{sd_ch3_end}: On the Thursday, Ms. Deniz sets the exam. She stands at the front with the papers face down and looks at the room for a moment longer than she needs to. "Turn them over," she says. "Good luck." It takes her ninety minutes of marking, that evening, to understand what has happened to her class.
keys.{sd_ch3_kerem_c0}: Sit down next to him and say nothing at all.
keys.{sd_ch3_kerem_c1}: "Twenty-second of November. I am free every evening until then."
keys.{sd_ch3_kerem_c2}: Match the joke. Keep the door welded.
keys.{sd_ch3_kerem_help}: He starts to make it a joke and cannot get there. "Every evening," he repeats, like he is checking the sentence for a trap. "You know I am going to be terrible at it." "Yes." "Fine." He shakes your hand, which he has never done in twelve years, and is immediately embarrassed about it.
keys.{sd_ch3_kerem_joke}: You give him the laugh he asked for and the moment closes over like water. He is so grateful for it that he buys you a drink from the machine that eats coins, and it eats the coin, and he laughs at that too, for slightly too long.
keys.{sd_ch3_kerem_sit}: Two minutes of nothing. Then, at normal volume, at last: "If I fail this one I am out in June with nothing and my father gets to be right for the rest of my life." He looks at the board. "That is it. That is the whole thing."
keys.{sd_ch3_kerem}: "Third year running," he announces before you can open your mouth. "They should name the resit after me." He is doing the voice. The one that means the subject is closed and the door is welded.
keys.{sd_ch3_list_c1}: Read the rest of the list properly first.
keys.{sd_ch3_list_c2}: Let him tell you in his own time.
keys.{sd_ch3_list}: Kerem is one of the three. He is on the far side of the hall, laughing at something, at a volume he does not normally use.
keys.{sd_ch3_names}: Kerem, and two others you barely know. Emre is not on the list - Emre is eleventh in the year - but Emre is standing in front of it doing sums on the back of his hand, and the sums are not marks. They have a currency symbol in front of them.
keys.{sd_ch3_open}: A crowd around the noticeboard on Friday, and the particular silence of people reading their own name. Three asterisks at the bottom of the sheet. Resit required. November the twenty-second.
keys.{sd_ch4_end}: You go out through the gate into a black four o'clock. The noticeboard still has the festival poster on it, curling worse now, and the scholarship line, still blank. Half the year gone. Everything that is going to matter has already been said out loud by somebody, at least once, to somebody.
keys.{sd_ch4_office}: She keeps you back at the end of the day. The office smells of cold tea and photocopier. Outside the window the yard is empty and the light is already going at half past four, because it is December now, and that happened while nobody was looking.
keys.{sd_ch4_open2}: Two days of nothing. Then a notice on the board with no explanation on it: 3-B, period one, attendance compulsory. The corridor outside that room is the quietest it has been since September.
keys.{sd_ch4_open}: Twenty-nine papers with the same three mistakes in them. Not similar. The same. Ms. Deniz marks until two in the morning, and then she marks the pile again from the bottom, because the first time through she had been hoping.
keys.{sd_ch5_end}: At the end of February the snow goes and the yard turns to mud, and somebody pins a new poster over the curled one by the door. Spring festival, the twenty-third of May. Underneath it the scholarship line - still blank, and now with about eleven weeks left for a name to be written on it.
keys.{sd_ch5_open2}: Six weeks of dark mornings, resits, and the particular boredom that makes people tell you things. Nobody is going anywhere. Everybody is available, if you go and find them.
keys.{sd_ch5_open}: January. The heating in 3-B works for about forty minutes a day and nobody has ever established when. Everyone comes back thinner and quieter. There is an empty desk at the back with nothing on it, and the class has silently agreed to route around it like a hole in the floor.
keys.{sd_ch6_end}: Wednesday morning. The eleventh of March. The corridor outside the meeting room smells of floor wax, exactly the way it did in September, and there are seven chairs along the wall and four of them are already taken.
keys.{sd_ch6_open}: March. Ms. Deniz writes four dates on the board and does not comment on any of them. The ninth: national portfolio competition, entries close. The tenth: resit, second and final sitting. The eleventh: hearing. The fifteenth: scholarship nominations close.
keys.{sd_ch6_pressure}: Three of those need the same thing: a reference from the class teacher, written properly, on school paper, before the deadline. And the class teacher is one woman with eleven other classes, a hearing to prepare for, and a statement in her coat pocket that she still has not signed.
keys.{sd_ch7_after}: Half past eleven on an ordinary Wednesday. Somewhere in the building a class is doing trigonometry. The corridor empties in four directions at once and every single person in it is having a different morning.
keys.{sd_ch7_end}: At four o'clock the building empties like any other Wednesday. Nine weeks to the festival. Whatever this year turns out to have been about, it stopped being decided this morning, and now all that is left is to find out what everybody does with it.
keys.{sd_ch7_hub_c0}: Emre. He is at the gate with his mother.
keys.{sd_ch7_hub_c1}: Ms. Deniz. She has a lesson in nine minutes.
keys.{sd_ch7_hub_c2}: Zeynep. She spoke, and now she has to go to lunch.
keys.{sd_ch7_hub_c3}: Kerem. The resit results came out at eleven.
keys.{sd_ch7_hub_c4}: Aylin. Nobody has seen her since nine o'clock this morning.
keys.{sd_ch7_hub}: You have got the rest of the day and one set of feet.
keys.{sd_ch7_open}: Four of the seven chairs are taken. Emre, in a blazer with mended cuffs and a tie he has clearly borrowed. Beside him a woman with her hands in her lap who has taken a day off work she cannot afford. Ms. Deniz, two pages in her hand. And Zeynep, who has not said one word since half past nine.
keys.{sd_ch7_wait_c1}: Go through it with Zeynep one more time.
keys.{sd_ch7_wait_c2}: Ask Ms. Deniz what is in the two pages.
keys.{sd_ch7_wait_c3}: Stand very still and go over your three sentences.
keys.{sd_ch7_wait}: Ten to ten. Somewhere inside the room a chair scrapes. There is nothing left to prepare and eleven minutes to not prepare it in.
keys.{sd_ch8_evening}: Dusk. Somebody gets the lantern strings working all at once and the whole yard goes gold and lets out a noise you can hear three streets away. Nine months ago you walked through that gate into a corridor that smelled of floor wax.
keys.{sd_ch8_open}: The twenty-third of May. Lanterns going up on wire across the yard, a stage made of scaffolding and optimism, and the smell of a hundred people cooking things badly. Whatever this year was, it is nearly over, and it is being decorated.
keys.{sd_ch8_prep_c0}: The gable wall. Aylin has been given four metres of it.
keys.{sd_ch8_prep_c1}: The stage rig. Kerem has taken it over and nobody stopped him.
keys.{sd_ch8_prep_c2}: The programme desk. Zeynep is running the whole running order.
keys.{sd_ch8_prep_c3}: The staff room. Ms. Deniz asked you to come and find her.
keys.{sd_ch8_prep_c4}: The gate. Somebody said they saw Emre outside it an hour ago.
keys.{sd_ch8_prep_c5}: The library. There are still exams after all this.
keys.{sd_ch8_prep}: Setup runs all afternoon and everybody is somewhere. Where are you?
keys.{sd_choose_partner_c2}: Ask Emre. Nobody else is going to.
keys.{sd_choose_partner_c3}: Ask Ms. Deniz to work alone.
keys.{sd_choose_partner}: Around you, chairs scrape as people pair off. Kerem is already half out of his seat. Aylin has not looked up. Emre has not been asked by anyone. Your move.
keys.{sd_confess2_c1}: "I will take mine. I am not doing his for him."
keys.{sd_confess2_c2}: "Ask him about the fees before you ask him anything else."
keys.{sd_confess2}: "Who sold them to you?" The pen waits over the second line.
keys.{sd_confess_hold}: "That is loyalty," she says, "and it is the expensive kind." She caps the pen. "I will find out anyway. It will take me a week, and for that week the whole class stays failed." She lets that sit. "Go to your lesson. I am not angry with you. I would like you to notice that I am not."
keys.{sd_confess_name}: She writes it down with no visible reaction at all and thanks you, and the whole thing takes eleven seconds. Emre is suspended by lunchtime. You get your detention, your resit and your clean slate, and all three of them feel exactly like they were paid for by somebody else.
keys.{sd_confess_self}: You expect fury. Instead Ms. Deniz just looks tired. "An honest coward is still honest," she says. "Detention, a resit, and a clean slate - if you earn it." She writes your name on a form. "And now the harder question."
keys.{sd_confess_why}: She stops writing. "Say that again." You do. She listens the whole way through without interrupting once, and at the end she puts the form in a drawer instead of the tray. "That is not a lighter punishment," she warns you. "It is a slower one. Slow is usually better and always harder."
keys.{sd_confront_emre_c1}: Glance at Zeynep. She was there in September too.
keys.{sd_confront_emre}: The room detonates. Emre lunges to his feet - but Ms. Deniz's voice cuts through everything: "SIT. DOWN." He sits. He is looking at you and there is nothing in his face at all, which is somehow the worst thing you have ever seen him do.
keys.{sd_corridor}: The hall smells like floor wax and wet coats. Somewhere ahead a voice is already mid-sentence, delivering the year's first headline to whoever is unlucky enough to be standing still.
keys.{sd_cover_up}: The term is salvaged only when a caretaker finds the rest of the stack behind the gym in December. Emre is suspended pending a hearing. Nobody ever asks you anything at all. That turns out to be much worse than being asked.
keys.{sd_date_all}: It takes four separate trips and a truly humiliating amount of pleading, and at half past eight there is one table in that yard with Kerem shouting on it, Zeynep's clipboard face down on it, Emre at the end of it being handed a plate, and Aylin drawing all of it on the back of the running order.
keys.{sd_date_aylin}: "Would you... go round with me?" you manage. Aylin's whole face lights like the lanterns. "I thought you were never going to ask," she breathes, and then, horrified at herself, "do not repeat that," and you walk in together and the night is already a different shape.
keys.{sd_date_emre}: He walks into the middle of the yard with you and about forty people notice at once and the noise dips for a second, and he keeps walking, which is the bravest thing you have seen anybody do all year. By the second hour somebody has handed him a plate and he is arguing with two people about optics.
keys.{sd_date_kerem}: Kerem throws an arm round you at the gate. "The whole crew. Last festival. Let us make it stupid and unforgettable." And you do: three hours of it, loudly, badly, in front of everyone, until your face aches from the laughing.
keys.{sd_date_solo}: You go round on your own with a paper cup, and it is fine - better than fine. You watch a school you have been inside for four years being briefly, ridiculously happy, and nobody needs anything from you for two whole hours.
keys.{sd_date_zeynep}: "I cannot, I am running the - " She looks at the clipboard. She looks at the yard. She puts the clipboard down on the desk, face down, with enormous care, like a woman putting down a weapon. "Actually," she says, "the running order can run itself for one hour."
keys.{sd_deniz_intro}: "Sit. All of you." Ms. Deniz drops a stack of papers on the desk. "This term: one group project, and one exam that decides your final grade. Choose your partner wisely. I will not referee your friendships."
keys.{sd_deniz_past_c1}: "Then why do you still make us do it?"
keys.{sd_deniz_past_c2}: "That is where the rule came from. Mistakes, not lies."
keys.{sd_deniz_past_right}: "That is what everybody says." She smiles at the mug. "It is a very comfortable sentence and it has never once helped. The right thing and the kind thing came apart in my hands that day, and nobody teaches you what to do when they do that."
keys.{sd_deniz_past_rule}: She looks at you for a long moment. "Nobody has ever worked that out before," she says. "Yes. I do not punish mistakes because nobody left my friend any room to have made one." She finishes the terrible tea. "Go home. It is dark and I am being unprofessional."
keys.{sd_deniz_past_wrong}: Her head comes up sharply, and then, slowly, she nods. "Because the alternative is a school where the strongest child decides what is true." A pause. "And because I keep hoping that if I do it enough times it will eventually feel like the right size. Twenty-six years. It has not."
keys.{sd_deniz_past}: "I was seventeen in this building," she says, apropos of nothing. "That window. That view." She turns the mug round on the desk. "I reported a friend of mine for something roughly this size. I was correct. She was expelled six weeks into the final year and she never went back to any school anywhere, and I have been losing an argument to a girl who is not in the room ever since."
keys.{sd_deniz_rule}: She lets the room settle, then says it like she says it every September, and means it more than she lets on. "One rule. I do not punish mistakes. Every one of you will make a spectacular one before June and I will help you carry it. I punish lying about them." Her eyes travel the room and do not hurry.
keys.{sd_deputy_accept}: "Good," he says warmly. "Good. I always said you were sensible." He writes your name on a form in front of you, upside down, so that you can watch it happen. It takes about nine seconds and it is the easiest thing that has happened to you all year.
keys.{sd_deputy_named}: Everything in his face stays exactly where it is, which is how you know. "That is an administrative document," he says, "and you should be extremely careful about where you claim to have seen it." A pause you could park a bus in. "Wednesday. Ten o'clock. I imagine you will want to prepare."
keys.{sd_deputy_offer2_c0}: "I am going to say all of it. Nominate whoever you like."
keys.{sd_deputy_offer2_c1}: "...I understand. I will keep it short."
keys.{sd_deputy_offer2_c2}: Agree with everything. Promise nothing you cannot take back.
keys.{sd_deputy_offer2_c3}: "You signed the handover form in June. It says the keys came back."
keys.{sd_deputy_offer2}: "Wednesday's hearing is a formality," he says. "The facts are not in dispute. What would be unhelpful - for the school, for the boy, frankly for you - is a lot of unrelated material about doors and keys and September." The pen taps once on your file. "Students who understand the difference between loyalty and noise tend to do very well here."
keys.{sd_deputy_offer}: On the Monday you are called to an office you have been inside twice in four years. The deputy head has your file open and a fountain pen he does not need. He is extremely pleasant. He asks after your family. He mentions, twice, that the scholarship nomination is at his discretion.
keys.{sd_deputy_play}: You agree with him nine times in four minutes and commit to nothing that could be quoted, and he is so pleased with the conversation that he never notices it did not contain a promise. In the corridor afterwards you realise you have just learned how the building actually works, and that you were unnervingly good at it.
keys.{sd_deputy_refuse}: The pleasantness does not go anywhere. It simply stops meaning anything, the way a light stays on in an empty room. "That is a great pity," he says, and closes your file, and thanks you for your time. Out in the corridor your hands are shaking and you cannot tell whether it is fear or the other thing.
keys.{sd_e_ask_n}: "Fees," he says, so fast it must have been sitting behind his teeth. "The second instalment. Due in November." Then he catches himself, and the shutter comes down hard. "Forget that. I am serious. If that gets into this school I will know exactly who put it there."
keys.{sd_e_car_n}: "I drive it. I do not own it." He does not look up. "It belongs to a man who pays me to move things across town on Saturdays. Ask your friend Zeynep, she will have a better version by Thursday." His pen has not stopped. "Page four is wrong, by the way. Fix it."
keys.{sd_e_deaf_n}: You look very hard at page four. He notices you noticing nothing, and something in his shoulders comes down half a centimetre. Later, packing up, he says: "You are alright." It is not a compliment. It is a status report.
keys.{sd_e_finish}: The project goes in and it is, by a distance, the best in the class. Ms. Deniz reads the front page twice to be sure of the second name. When she hands it back she says "Good work, both of you," and Emre puts it straight in his bag without looking at the grade.
keys.{sd_e_p1_c0}: "So where did the car come from?"
keys.{sd_e_p1_c1}: "You do not want to go home, do you?"
keys.{sd_e_p1}: He is brutally efficient. Sources sorted, argument mapped, the whole spine of the thing built in ninety minutes. He is also still there at seven in the evening, and at eight, with no sign of leaving, and no sign of anywhere to go.
keys.{sd_e_p2}: His phone goes. He takes it into the stacks and you can hear the shape of it if not the words - low, flat, repeating a number three times, then a long silence, then "I said I would handle it." He comes back and picks up exactly where he left off, as though nothing happened.
keys.{sd_e_stay_n}: The pen stops. It is the first time all year that anything has stopped him. "The library is warm and it has a light," he says, to the table. "That is the entire reason. Do not make it a story." Then, quieter: "You are the second person to notice. The first one was the librarian."
keys.{sd_e_work_n}: You work in silence for two hours and it is the least exhausting company you have had all week. At one point he slides a corrected page back to you without comment, and it is corrected kindly, which you did not know he could do.
keys.{sd_emre_deniz}: "A fund." His face does something complicated and awful. "There is a fund." Very quietly: "Four years. Nobody said that to me once in four years." He does not promise you anything. But he stops fanning the papers, and puts them inside his jacket, and the arithmetic goes out of his eyes.
keys.{sd_emre_falls}: Emre's printouts are found in his locker within the hour. Suspended, pending a board hearing in the spring. The class exhales like a held breath. "Thank you," Ms. Deniz says quietly, only to you. She does not look thankful. She looks like a woman who has now watched the same thing happen twice in one lifetime.
keys.{sd_emre_impress}: "It is on the noticeboard. It has been on the noticeboard since Friday." A beat. "Nobody reads anything in this school." He sits down at the back, where he can see the whole room and nobody can see his desk.
keys.{sd_emre_intro_c2}: Say nothing. Note the mended cuffs.
keys.{sd_emre_intro}: The board still has last term's timetable on it. Emre crosses the room, wipes one line with the side of his fist and rewrites it - correctly - before anyone has told him to. He does not look pleased with himself. He looks like someone doing a job. His blazer is last year's and the cuffs have been mended.
keys.{sd_emre_needle}: "Nobody has ever thought that about me," he says, without turning around, "and I would like to keep it that way." The class laughs. He does not.
keys.{sd_emre_none}: "No," he agrees. "Nobody does." He squares the stack of paper on his knee, neatly, the way he does everything. "Thank you for not lying about it. That is genuinely more than I get from most people." And he goes back to work.
keys.{sd_emre_note}: Mended, not replaced. Neat stitches, done by someone patient. Emre drives a car he could not possibly afford and wears a blazer somebody sat up sewing. You file it away without knowing why.
keys.{sd_emre_stop}: "You will help me." He says it like a foreign phrase. Then: "Twenty-nine copies are already out there. I cannot un-sell those." He looks at the remainder in his hands for a long time. "But I can stop at twenty-nine." He does not burn them in front of you. But on Monday there are none left to buy.
keys.{sd_emre_suspend}: Suspended anyway, pending a hearing in the spring. There is no version of this where he stays in the building. But the file that goes upstairs has two pages in it instead of one, and the second page is the one that will matter in March.
keys.{sd_emre_threat}: Emre's grin curdles. "Report me and I will bury you with it. Everyone saw you come back here, hero." He shoves past, slamming his shoulder into yours. Six steps away he stops, and does not turn round, and says: "You have no idea what this is for." Then he keeps walking.
keys.{sd_emre_why2_c0}: "Burn them. I will help you find the other option."
keys.{sd_emre_why2_c1}: "Ms. Deniz. There is a hardship fund. She will not tell the board."
keys.{sd_emre_why2_c2}: "I do not have one. I am sorry."
keys.{sd_emre_why2}: "So this is what is left," he says, and holds the papers up like evidence against himself. "Do not tell me it is wrong. I know it is wrong. Tell me what the other option is and I will take it."
keys.{sd_emre_why}: The stack of paper comes down. For a moment he genuinely cannot speak. "Eleven thousand," he says. "By November. Then again in April." A dry laugh at nothing. "My mother mends my blazer so I do not look like the boy whose fees are late. She thinks I have a job at the garage. I do have a job at the garage. It is not enough."
keys.{sd_ending_accounts}:
"Stop keeping accounts," you tell him. "We are just friends now. It is allowed." He looks at you as though you have proposed something physically impossible. It takes him about four years to fully accept the arrangement, during which he keeps trying to pay for things, and you keep letting him, because that is how he says it.

- ENDING: Close the Book -
keys.{sd_ending_alone}:
The festival roars on without you and that is all right. You watch the lanterns go up into the dark one at a time, make a quiet promise about next year to nobody in particular, and go home while the music is still playing. Not every year has to be one you tell people about.

- ENDING: One More Year -
keys.{sd_ending_ashes}:
You add it up honestly, on a roof, at eleven at night, and it comes to this: a boy excluded, a teacher reprimanded, a girl who stopped drawing, a friend who sat the same exam three times on his own - and one envelope in your pocket with your name on it. She told you in September. She never once punished a mistake. This was not a mistake, and you have known that since November.

- ENDING: What It Cost -
keys.{sd_ending_brothers}:
Kerem clinks his bottle against yours. "Us against the world, remember?" "Always," you say, and mean it. He does the two years. He is the best in his cohort by a distance and utterly insufferable about it. Grades fade. Marks fade. Twelve years of somebody knowing exactly which joke you need does not.

- ENDING: Brothers in Arms -
keys.{sd_ending_calling}:
"Give me your number. I am going to be the one who phones." She writes it on the back of the running order and hands it over like a dare. You phone on the Tuesday. She does not pick up until the fourth ring, on purpose, and then talks for fifty minutes. Eleven years later she still does not pick up until the fourth ring.

- ENDING: Four Rings -
keys.{sd_ending_class}:
"Nothing ends tonight," you tell them. "We just stop being in the same building." Kerem says that is the most pretentious sentence he has ever heard and then repeats it twice more before midnight. Four of them make it to the August meet-up. Three make it the year after. Two are still there at thirty, and one of them is on the roof of an entirely different building, telling this story.

- ENDING: The Class of Pinar -
keys.{sd_ending_firsttable}:
You ask her a question about herself, and then another, and then another, for an hour, and she answers all of them badly and then better, because nobody has done this to her since she was thirteen and she is dreadfully out of practice. At about midnight she stops mid-sentence and says, "This is the first time anybody has sat at my table on purpose."

- ENDING: The First Table -
keys.{sd_ending_golden}:
"Aylin - it was always you." She laughs, eyes wet, and takes your hand, and says, "Four hours on a bus," and you say, "I can read on a bus," and that is the entire negotiation. She gets the place in September. You are on the platform with a bag of her brushes. Some years you survive. This one you lived.

- ENDING: The Golden Year -
keys.{sd_ending_honors}:
The letter is real in your hands and the answer is yes. You earned every line of it, alone, in the quiet, while a building full of people had the worst and best year of their lives four metres below the window you were working at. It opens an enormous door. It cost you the year that was happening at the time.

- ENDING: Lonely Honours -
keys.{sd_ending_lastlight}:
Nobody makes a speech. You sit on a warm roof in the dark for an hour with four people who all know exactly what it cost each other to get here, and it does not need saying, and none of you says it. Aylin draws until the light goes. Then somebody suggests chips, and that is how the year ends: badly lit, unceremonious, complete.

- ENDING: The Last of the Light -
keys.{sd_ending_ledger}:
"Then do it for somebody else. That is how you pay it back." He turns that over like a coin he is checking for weight. Nine years later there is a small hardship fund at a technical college with no name attached to it, administered quietly by a man who insists it is not a big deal and becomes extremely irritable if you mention it.

- ENDING: Paid Forward -
keys.{sd_ending_longway}:
"Say it back to me." It takes him three goes, and on the third one he gets the whole sentence out without laughing: I was never the stupid one. He is very quiet after that. Six years later he owns two units on the industrial road and employs four people, and there is a form on his office wall, framed, that a teacher signed in March.

- ENDING: The Long Way Round -
keys.{sd_ending_paper}:
"Then go," you tell her. "Four hours is a bus, not a wall." She looks at you for a long moment and neither of you says the thing you both nearly said. In September she goes. She sends you a photograph of her first studio wall, and you keep it, and it is never quite said out loud - but she got out, and part of that was you, and you would do it again.

- ENDING: Paper and Distance -
keys.{sd_ending_saturday}:
"Forty kilometres," you tell him. "I will be on the Saturday bus." He says you absolutely will not. You absolutely do - not every week, but enough weeks, for two years, which turns out to be the whole difference between a friendship that ended at eighteen and one that did not. He never thanks you for it. He never has to.

- ENDING: The Saturday Bus -
keys.{sd_ending_secondchance}:
"You did the hard part," you tell him. "I said a number out loud in a room. You stood up in front of your mother." He does not argue, which from Emre is agreement. He passes his exams in a room full of strangers. Two years later, part-time, paid for by himself, exactly the way he said. He was never the villain of this year. He was just the first one to run out of options.

- ENDING: The Second Chance -
keys.{sd_ending_shadow}:
You leave the way guilt teaches you to: quietly, alone, down the back stairs, before the lights can find your face. The gate clicks shut behind you and the music carries on without any noticeable difference. Some doors get closed on you. This one you closed yourself, all year, one small silence at a time.

- ENDING: The Long Shadow -
keys.{sd_ending_smaller}:
"Stay," you say. "There are places here too." And she does. She takes the local course, and she is kind about it, and she never once blames you out loud. Four years later she is very good at something adjacent to the thing she was extraordinary at, and every so often she stops mid-sentence and looks out of a window, and you have learned not to ask.

- ENDING: The Smaller Life -
keys.{sd_ending_together}:
You go round all four of them out loud, one at a time, and say the actual thing. Kerem tries to make it a joke twice and fails twice. Zeynep cries and is extremely angry about crying. Emre listens to his with his eyes shut. Aylin does not say anything at all - she just turns the page round, and it is all five of you, drawn in the last ten minutes, on a roof.

- ENDING: Say It Out Loud -
keys.{sd_ending_zeynep}:
"You are the person who stood up at that hearing," you tell her, "with your name on it, when it cost you everything you had built." She thinks about that for a long time. "Huh," she says eventually. "That is a much better one." She studies law. Of course she studies law. She is going to be terrifying.

- ENDING: On the Record -
keys.{sd_festival_roof}: At half past ten the music drops to the slow songs and the rooftop door does what it has done all year, which is open. Up here the whole city is doing something else entirely. Below, the lanterns. One hour left of the last day of the last year.
keys.{sd_fin_all_n_c0}: "Nothing ends tonight. We just stop being in the same building."
keys.{sd_fin_all_n_c1}: Say what each of them did for you. Out loud. All four.
keys.{sd_fin_all_n_c2}: Say nothing. Let it be an hour instead of a speech.
keys.{sd_fin_all_n}: It takes twenty minutes to get all of them up the stairs and one of them is technically not allowed in the building. Kerem on the parapet with his arms out. Zeynep with no clipboard. Emre sitting against the stairwell exactly where he sat in October. Aylin drawing, fast, because the light is going. Somebody says: so what happens now?
keys.{sd_fin_alone_n_c1}: Watch the lanterns. Go home when it is over.
keys.{sd_fin_alone_n_c2}: Go down the back stairs before anybody sees you.
keys.{sd_fin_alone_n_c3}: Add it up honestly. All of it.
keys.{sd_fin_alone_n}: Nobody follows you up. Below, the whole school is having the night it will talk about for ten years. The envelope from the staff room is still in your pocket, and so is everything else you did and did not do since September.
keys.{sd_fin_aylin_n_c1}: "Then go. Four hours is a bus, not a wall."

keys.{sd_fin_kerem_n_c2}: "Forty kilometres. I will be on the Saturday bus."
keys.{sd_fin_kerem_n}: He comes up with two bottles of something fizzy and non-alcoholic and an expression of enormous satisfaction. keys.{sd_fin_zeynep_n_c0}: "You are the person who stood up at that hearing."
keys.{sd_fin_zeynep_n_c1}: Ask her a question about herself. Then another. Then another.
keys.{sd_fin_zeynep_n_c2}: "Give me your number. I am going to be the one who phones."
keys.{sd_fin_zeynep_n}: She comes up last, after the running order is genuinely finished, and sits down with her shoes off. "Nobody came looking for me," she says. "Which is fine. keys.{sd_finale_hub_c0}: Everyone. The whole ridiculous year, in one place.
keys.{sd_finale_hub_c5}: Nobody. That is what a roof is for.
keys.{sd_finale_hub}: However this year ends, it ends in the next hour, on this roof. Who is up here with you?
keys.{sd_first_bell}: The day goes the way first days go: six lessons of being told what June will cost you. Then the last bell, and the building empties like a bath. Coats, shouting, somebody's bag splitting on the stairs. Day one, survived. Two hundred and eleven to go.
keys.{sd_first_step_c0}: Straight up the middle. Let them look.
keys.{sd_first_step_c1}: Along the wall, where you can see everyone.
keys.{sd_first_step_c2}: Past all of it. First one to the classroom.
keys.{sd_first_step}: Four years you have walked through this gate. Today it feels like a starting line. How do you go in?
keys.{sd_fs_bold_n}: You walk it like a corridor you own. A couple of first-years get out of your way without deciding to. It costs nothing to look certain. You have gotten very good at it.
keys.{sd_fs_early_n}: You are through the doors before the bell has finished. The building is still cool and empty and it belongs to you for about ninety seconds. Nine months. One name on that list.
keys.{sd_fs_quiet_n}: You take the shaded side and read the crowd instead of joining it. Who is laughing too loudly. Who is walking alone and pretending it was the plan. You always see more from the edge.
keys.{sd_hear_deputy2}: He is magnificent about it for about ninety seconds. Then he asks for the hearing to be adjourned on a point of procedure, and the chair - an outside governor who has been checking her watch since ten past ten - says, "No, I do not think we will," and asks the minute-taker to read the last entry back.
keys.{sd_hear_deputy}: The room goes completely silent. The chair says, "I beg your pardon?" So you say it again, slowly, with the date on it: the fourteenth of June, the handover form, keys returned, signed. And you say who signed it. Beside you Zeynep makes a very small noise. Ms. Deniz does not move a muscle.
keys.{sd_hear_fees}: You say the number. Then the date. Then the second date, in April, and the garage on Saturdays, and the blazer that got mended instead of replaced. The room's temperature changes. Beside you Emre says, very quietly, "Do not," and you keep going, and his mother puts one hand flat on the table and leaves it there.
keys.{sd_hear_keys}: "Nothing was forced," you say. "There is no damage to the door because there was never a lock to break. Mr. Halil retired in August and his keys were never collected." keys.{sd_hear_nothing}: "No. Nothing to add." Four words. The minute-taker types them. The chair says thank you and moves on and the entire thing is over in the time it takes to boil a kettle. Beside you Ms. Deniz's two pages stay face down on the table and are never read.
keys.{sd_hear_short}: Eleven words. The minute-taker types them in about two seconds. Nobody asks you a follow-up question, because you have not left anywhere for one to go. Emre does not look at you. That is somehow the part you will remember: that he did not even look.
keys.{sd_hear_whole}: It takes you nine minutes and you do not stop once. September. The keys. The fees. The twenty-nine of us, including whichever of us was too frightened to say so. keys.{sd_hearing_open}: The room is smaller than it should be. A table, five adults, a jug of water nobody touches, and a minute-taker with a laptop. Is there anything you would like to add?"
keys.{sd_hearing_you_c0}: "It was Emre. He sold the answers. That is all I know."
keys.{sd_hearing_you_c1}: "He needed eleven thousand lira by November. Ask him why."
keys.{sd_hearing_you_c2}: "Nothing was forced. That office has been open since June."

keys.{sd_hearing_you_c4}: "Before I answer - ask him who signed the June handover form."

keys.{sd_intro2}: Room 3-B smells of chalk and cheap cologne. You drop into your usual seat by the window. One year left. Better make it count.
keys.{sd_k_coast_n}: "Finally, sense." He puts his feet on the desk. The relief on his face is one size too big for the decision, and you notice, and you let it go.
keys.{sd_k_finish}: The project goes in on time. Kerem builds the model for it out of scrap aluminium in one evening and it is, objectively, the best physical object anyone hands to Ms. Deniz that term. Nobody grades that part.
keys.{sd_k_p1_c0}: "We can actually win this if we try, you know."
keys.{sd_k_p1_c1}: "Let us just coast. It is senior year."

keys.{sd_march_hub_c1}: Kerem. He sat the resit this morning and has not spoken since.
keys.{sd_march_hub_c2}: Zeynep. She has been asked to give evidence and she is terrified.
keys.{sd_march_hub_c3}: Emre. Nobody should spend the night before their own hearing alone.

keys.{sd_s_p1_c1}: Take a break. Find someone. Anyone.

keys.{sd_w1_kerem2_c0}: "You are extraordinary at this. That is just a fact."
keys.{sd_w1_kerem2_c1}: "Who told you it was a choice between two lives?"
keys.{sd_w1_kerem2_c2}: "The resit was the twenty-second of November. What happened?"

keys.{sd_w1_zeynep2_c0}: "Stand with me at lunch. In the middle, where they can see."
keys.{sd_w1_zeynep2_c1}: "So stop. You do not have to be the one who knows things."
keys.{sd_w1_zeynep2_c2}: "What actually happened in June? All of it."
keys.{sd_w1_zeynep2}: "It is very funny, actually," she says, in a voice with no funny anywhere in it. "I have been handing them ammunition for four years and it took them about nine days to work out which way round to hold it." She shrugs. "I am not going to cry about it. I built the gun."

keys.{sd_w2_deniz_c1}: "Protect your job. Nobody else is going to protect it for you."
keys.{sd_w2_deniz_c2}: "Ask me instead what I am going to do on the eleventh."

keys.{sd_wait_still}: Three sentences. You go through them the way you would go through a phone number you cannot afford to lose. Down the corridor a door opens and a man's voice says a name that is not yours in a tone of complete comfort.
keys.{sd_wait_zeynep}: She has the sentences written on the back of a receipt, which she has folded and unfolded so many times it is coming apart at the crease. "Say it slowly," you tell her. She does. It is steady. "Again." It is steady again. "Okay," she says. "Okay. I hate this. Okay."
keys.{sd_walk_alone}: You take the long way, past the sports field, where nobody talks to you and nobody needs anything. Some days that is the best part.
keys.{sd_walk_aylin}: She walks half a step behind until you slow down enough that it stops being possible. At the gate she says, out of nowhere, "You looked at the branch first. Not the building." Then she goes red and leaves.
keys.{sd_walk_home_c2}: Walk out with Zeynep for once.
keys.{sd_walk_home_c3}: Alone. It has been a long day.
keys.{sd_walk_home}: The gate is a hundred metres away and you can cross it with anybody you like.
keys.{sd_walk_kerem}: He talks the entire way about a motorbike engine he rebuilt over the summer - carburettor, timing, the exact noise it made when it finally caught. He is articulate, precise and completely certain, and it is the only subject all day where he has sounded like that.
keys.{sd_walk_zeynep}: She talks the whole way, and then at the corner she stops and says, "Nobody walks with me. They call me and then they hang up." She laughs immediately, so you will treat it as a joke. You could. She is giving you the option on purpose.
keys.{sd_week_bridge}: Midterms come and go. You are finding your footing here - but the halls have started to hum with a rumour that will not die, and it has been getting louder every day since the resit list went up.

keys.{sd_winter_hub1_c0}: Aylin. Nobody has seen her sketchbook since November.
keys.{sd_winter_hub1_c1}: Kerem. He has been at the shop every weekend since December.
keys.{sd_winter_hub1_c2}: Zeynep. For once, nobody is talking to her.
keys.{sd_winter_hub1_c3}: Ms. Deniz. Her office light is on and it is Saturday.
keys.{sd_winter_hub1_c4}: Emre. He is suspended, not dead. Somebody should go.
keys.{sd_winter_hub1_c5}: Nobody. You have got a term to catch up on.
keys.{sd_winter_hub1}: A free Saturday. It is not enough time to do everything, and the thing about January is that whoever you do not go and see spends it alone.
keys.{sd_winter_hub2_c0}: Aylin. The portfolio statement is still not written.

keys.{sd_winter_hub2_c5}: Your own final year. Somebody has to look after it.

keys.{sd_zeynep_brush}: "It is eight in the morning and I already know more than you will all year," she says, cheerful, and peels off toward another target. The smile does not go anywhere. That is how you know it is load-bearing.
keys.{sd_zeynep_intro_c0}: Listen properly. She is enjoying this too much to be fine.
keys.{sd_zeynep_intro_c1}: "What have you got that nobody else has?"
keys.{sd_zeynep_intro_c2}: "Zeynep. It is eight in the morning."

keys.{sd_zeynep_listen}: You let her finish. Then you ask how her summer was. She blinks - actually blinks - like the question is in a language she half remembers. "Fine," she says. "Quiet." And for one second she is not performing, and you see it: quiet was not a good thing.
